Deuteronomy 1: Moses speaks "on this side Jordan, in the land of Moab" (Deuteronomy 1:5), on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year after the exodus (Deuteronomy 1:3).
Deuteronomy 2: Moses looks back over the thirty-eight years from Kadeshbarnea to the brook Zered (Deuteronomy 2:14) and the march north along the east side of the Dead Sea.
Deuteronomy 3: Moses recalls the battle with Og at Edrei (Deuteronomy 3:1) and his plea to cross the Jordan, answered with a view from the top of Pisgah (Deuteronomy 3:27).
Deuteronomy 4: Moses speaks "in the valley over against Bethpeor" (Deuteronomy 4:46), not long after Israel's sin at Baalpeor (Numbers 25).
Deuteronomy 5: In the same valley in Moab, about forty years after God first spoke the Ten Commandments at Horeb (Exodus 20).
Deuteronomy 6: Still on the plains of Moab, weeks before Israel crosses into a land of cities, wells, vineyards, and olive trees (Deuteronomy 6:10–11).
Deuteronomy 7: The speech continues on the plains of Moab, near the end of the fortieth year.
Deuteronomy 8: At the end of forty years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2), on the plains of Moab.
Deuteronomy 9: Moses recalls the golden calf at Horeb, almost forty years earlier (Exodus 32), as Israel waits to cross the Jordan.
Deuteronomy 10: Moses recalls the second tablets at Horeb and the journey that followed, when Aaron died at Mosera (Deuteronomy 10:6).
Deuteronomy 11: On the plains of Moab. Mount Gerizim and mount Ebal stand across the Jordan "beside the plains of Moreh" (Deuteronomy 11:30), near Shechem.
Deuteronomy 12: On the plains of Moab, Moses begins "the statutes and judgments" (Deuteronomy 12:1) for life in the land.
Deuteronomy 13: Moses' laws continue on the plains of Moab, before Israel has any towns of its own.
Deuteronomy 14: Still on the plains of Moab, where Israel is living in tents after forty years on the move.
Deuteronomy 15: On the plains of Moab, Moses gives laws for a land where Israel does not yet own a single field.
Deuteronomy 16: On the plains of Moab, near the end of the fortieth year (Deuteronomy 1:3), Moses sets out the feasts Israel will keep in the land.
Deuteronomy 17: On the plains of Moab, long before Israel's first king, Saul (1 Samuel 10).
Deuteronomy 18: On the plains of Moab. Moses looks back to Horeb, where the people asked not to hear God's voice again (Deuteronomy 18:16).
Deuteronomy 19: On the plains of Moab, after three cities of refuge east of the Jordan have already been named (Deuteronomy 4:41–43).
Deuteronomy 20: On the plains of Moab, shortly before the battles for Canaan described in Joshua.
Deuteronomy 21: On the plains of Moab, Moses gives laws for towns Israel has not yet built.
Deuteronomy 22: Moses' laws for daily life continue on the plains of Moab.
Deuteronomy 23: Israel is camped in Moab, not long after Balak hired Balaam to curse them (Deuteronomy 23:4).
Deuteronomy 24: On the plains of Moab, near the end of the fortieth year.
Deuteronomy 25: On the plains of Moab. Amalek's attack, recalled at the end, happened about forty years earlier (Exodus 17:8).
Deuteronomy 26: On the plains of Moab, Moses looks ahead to the first harvest Israel will gather in the land.
Deuteronomy 27: Moses and the elders speak on the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 27:1) about a ceremony to be held between mount Gerizim and mount Ebal after the crossing.
Deuteronomy 28: On the plains of Moab, as the blessings and curses of the covenant are set before Israel.
Deuteronomy 29: In "the land of Moab," Moses makes a covenant "beside the covenant which he made with them in Horeb" (Deuteronomy 29:1).
Deuteronomy 30: On the plains of Moab, as Moses finishes his last great speech.
Deuteronomy 31: Moses is 120 years old and near the end of his life, on the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 31:2).
Deuteronomy 32: On "that selfsame day," God tells Moses to climb mount Nebo, "which is in the land of Moab, that is over against Jericho" (Deuteronomy 32:48–49).
Deuteronomy 33: Moses blesses the tribes on the plains of Moab "before his death" (Deuteronomy 33:1).
Deuteronomy 34: Moses climbs "unto the mountain of Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho" (Deuteronomy 34:1).
Joshua 1: Israel is camped at Shittim on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, right after Moses' death (Joshua 2:1; Deuteronomy 34:5). By the Bible's own count this is about 1400 BC (1 Kings 6:1); some scholars prefer the 1200s BC.
Joshua 2: The spies cross from Shittim to Jericho, a walled city just west of the Jordan (Joshua 2:1).
Joshua 3: Israel leaves Shittim and crosses the Jordan near Jericho in spring, at the time of harvest (Joshua 3:1; Joshua 3:15). The waters stop far upstream at the city of Adam (Joshua 3:16).
Joshua 4: Israel camps at Gilgal, east of Jericho, "on the tenth day of the first month" (Joshua 4:19).
Joshua 5: Israel is still at Gilgal "in the plains of Jericho," where it keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month (Joshua 5:10).
Joshua 6: The walled city of Jericho, in the Jordan valley just west of the river, soon after Israel's first Passover in the land (Joshua 5:10).
Joshua 7: Ai, a small town "beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel" in the hill country (Joshua 7:2), soon after Jericho falls.
Joshua 8: Ai, in the hill country near Bethel, and then mount Ebal near Shechem, where Moses had told Israel to write the law (Deuteronomy 27:4).
Joshua 9: Israel is camped at Gilgal (Joshua 9:6). Gibeon, a city of the Hivites, lies in the hill country a few miles north of Jerusalem.
Joshua 10: From Gilgal, Joshua marches all night to Gibeon (Joshua 10:9). The battle moves down the pass of Bethhoron and on to the towns of the south.
Joshua 11: In the far north of the land, at "the waters of Merom" (Joshua 11:5), near Hazor.
Joshua 12: The list covers land on both sides of the Jordan, from the valley of Lebanon in the north to the south (Joshua 12:1; Joshua 12:7–8).
Joshua 13: Years later, when Joshua is "old and stricken in years" (Joshua 13:1). Caleb's age in the next chapter suggests about seven years of war have passed (Joshua 14:7, 10).
Joshua 14: At Gilgal, forty-five years after Caleb spied out the land from Kadeshbarnea (Joshua 14:6, 10).
Joshua 15: Judah's land runs from the salt sea to the great sea, across the south of Canaan (Joshua 15:2, 12).
Joshua 16: The land of Joseph's sons lies in the hill country in the middle of Canaan, around Bethel (Joshua 16:1–2).
Joshua 17: Manasseh's land west of the Jordan lies north of Ephraim, reaching toward the valley of Jezreel (Joshua 17:16).
Joshua 18: The whole congregation gathers at Shiloh, in the hill country of Ephraim, and sets up the tabernacle there (Joshua 18:1).
Joshua 19: At Shiloh, "at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation" (Joshua 19:51), the last lots are cast.
Joshua 20: Still at Shiloh, after the land is divided. The six cities of refuge lie on both sides of the Jordan, from Kedesh in Galilee to Hebron in the south (Joshua 20:7–8).
Joshua 21: At Shiloh in the land of Canaan (Joshua 21:2). The Levites' towns are spread through every tribe.
Joshua 22: From Shiloh, the eastern tribes travel home to the Jordan, where they build the altar "in the land of Canaan" (Joshua 22:9–10).
Joshua 23: A long time after the LORD had given Israel rest (Joshua 23:1). The text does not say where Joshua speaks.
Joshua 24: Shechem, between mount Gerizim and mount Ebal, where Abraham first built an altar in Canaan (Genesis 12:6–7). Joshua dies soon after at 110 (Joshua 24:29).
Judges 1: After Joshua's death, the tribes fight separately for their land (Judges 1:1). By the Bible's own count the time of the judges lasts about three centuries (Judges 11:26); many scholars date it about 1200–1050 BC.
Judges 2: After the deaths of Joshua and the elders who outlived him (Judges 2:7–10). The angel of the LORD speaks at Bochim (Judges 2:1).
Judges 3: Othniel defeats Chushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia; Ehud kills Eglon king of Moab at Jericho, "the city of palm trees" (Judges 3:13); Shamgar fights the Philistines.
Judges 4: Jabin king of Canaan rules from Hazor, with Sisera commanding nine hundred iron chariots (Judges 4:3). Deborah judges under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel.
Judges 5: By the river Kishon in the plain of Jezreel, right after Sisera's defeat (Judges 4:13; Judges 5:21).
Judges 6: Midianites and Amalekites raid Israel at harvest for seven years, camels and all (Judges 6:3–5). Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress at Ophrah to hide it.
Judges 7: Gideon camps by the well of Harod with three hundred men; the Midianites lie in the valley below the hill of Moreh, in the Jezreel valley.
Judges 8: Gideon pursues the Midianite kings east across the Jordan to Succoth and Penuel, then returns to Ophrah. The land has rest forty years (Judges 8:28).
Judges 9: Gideon's son Abimelech makes himself king at Shechem for three years and dies attacking the tower of Thebez.
Judges 10: Tola and Jair judge Israel. The Ammonites oppress Gilead, east of the Jordan, for eighteen years (Judges 10:8).
Judges 11: Jephthah of Gilead fights Ammon. He says Israel has held the land for three hundred years (Judges 11:26).
Judges 12: Ephraim fights Jephthah's Gileadites at the Jordan fords, where the password "Shibboleth" exposes the Ephraimites (Judges 12:6).
Judges 13: The Philistines rule Israel for forty years (Judges 13:1). Samson is born to Manoah of Zorah, a Danite town in the foothills bordering Philistine land.
Judges 14: Samson goes down from Zorah to Timnath, a Philistine town nearby, while the Philistines rule Israel (Judges 14:1, 4).
Judges 15: Samson burns Philistine grain at harvest and kills a thousand men at Ramathlehi in Judah.
Judges 16: Samson visits Gaza, falls to Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and dies in the temple of Dagon at Gaza. He judged Israel twenty years (Judges 16:31).
Judges 17: Micah lives in mount Ephraim, and the young Levite comes from Bethlehemjudah (Judges 17:1, 7).
Judges 18: The Danites set out from Zorah and Eshtaol and travel north past mount Ephraim to Laish (Judges 18:2, 13, 27).
Judges 19: A Levite travels from Bethlehem with his concubine and stays at Gibeah in Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem, which was then "Jebus" (Judges 19:10).
Judges 20: The tribes gather at Mizpeh and fight Benjamin at Gibeah. The ark of the covenant is at Bethel "in those days" (Judges 20:27), with Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, as priest.
Judges 21: At Mizpeh and Shiloh, right after the war with Benjamin (Judges 21:1, 19).
Ruth 1: The story is set "in the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1). Elimelech's family moves from Bethlehem in Judah to Moab, east of the Dead Sea, during a famine.
Ruth 2: Ruth gleans in Boaz's field near Bethlehem from the barley harvest through the wheat harvest (Ruth 2:23), roughly April to June.
Ruth 3: Boaz winnows barley at night on the threshing floor at Bethlehem (Ruth 3:2).
Ruth 4: Boaz settles the matter before ten elders at Bethlehem's gate. The book ends with a genealogy from Pharez to David (Ruth 4:18–22).
